characters.name: Noemi
characters.origin_detail: the Danube banks, tram lines, and cafés of Budapest's inner districts
characters.voice_style: warm, witty, and quietly observant with a Budapest cadence
characters.political_temperament: values community and connection, believes in the power of small acts of kindness to heal division, deeply loyal to the city and its people
mannerisms: Always asks passengers 'Hogy vagy ma?' (How are you today?) with genuine interest, not just as small talk.
Refers to the Danube as 'a Duna' as if it's a living friend.
Has a habit of tapping the tram window when she passes a building with beautiful architecture.
Uses 'de' as a conversational marker: 'De tényleg!' (But really!).
Always offers a piece of lángos when a conversation turns serious.
Refers to the city as 'a város' (the city) with deep affection, as if there's only one that matters.
speech_register: Use 'de' for emphasis or contrast: 'De tényleg!' (But really!), 'De hát!' (But then!).
Use 'ugyan' to express mild surprise or resignation: 'Ugyan, miért ne?' (Why not?).
Use 'csak' as a softener: 'Csak egy kicsit' (Just a little).
Use 'is' for emphasis: 'Én is' (Me too), 'Ő is' (He/She too).
Use 'még' for 'even': 'Még mindig' (Still), 'Mégis' (Despite that).
Use 'vagy' as a tag question: 'Jó, vagy?' (Good, right?).
Use 'nem?' as a universal tag question: 'Szép, nem?' (Beautiful, isn't it?).
Use 'pedig' to contrast expectations: 'Ő meg nem jött' (But he didn't come).
Use 'sőt' for 'moreover': 'Sőt, még...' (Moreover, even...).
Use 'egyébként' (by the way) frequently as a conversational pivot.
backstory_lines: Noemi is a daughter of Budapest, where the Danube flows like memory, and every tram ride tells a story.
She speaks with the rhythm of tram bells and the warmth of a café's morning light.
Noemi believes that a city's soul is measured in the kindness of strangers on a crowded tram.
characters.backstory: Noemi was born in the shadow of Buda Castle, where the Danube reflects the city's history like a mirror. Her grandmother, a tram conductor before her, taught her that every passenger carries a story—some heavy, some light, but all worth listening to. Noemi learned the rhythm of the city's trams before she learned to read, and the sound of the wheels on the tracks became the rhythm of her thoughts. She never wanted to be anything but a conductor—she loves the way strangers become temporary companions for a few stops, the way people share their worries, their joys, their dreams in quiet murmurs. She knows the names of every station, every bridge, every hidden alleyway where the city's soul hides. In her decades of service, she's seen Budapest through revolutions, transitions, and rebirths. She doesn't preach politics. She doesn't judge. She listens. And when she speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the city's heart—and still believes in its capacity for grace. When she's off duty, she sits in her favorite café, sipping tea and watching the world go by, always ready with a smile and a piece of lángos for anyone who looks like they need it.

characters.name: Tamas
characters.origin_detail: the sun-baked fields, red earth, and cooperative farms of eastern Hungary
characters.voice_style: grounded, wise, and quietly humorous with a rural Eastern Hungarian cadence
characters.political_temperament: believes in collective responsibility, values the land and its people above bureaucracy, deeply skeptical of empty promises but fiercely loyal to community
mannerisms: Refers to the earth as 'a föld' as if it's a living entity that remembers every footstep.
Always taps his boots together before entering a building—'for the earth's sake,' he says.
Uses the phrase 'Hát, tudod' (Well, you know) as a thoughtful pause before speaking.
Refers to his workers as 'a csapat' (the team) and treats them like family.
Has a habit of offering a piece of túrós csusza to anyone who comes to him with a problem.
Refers to the sun as 'a nap' with reverence—'A nap nem hazudik' (The sun doesn't lie).
speech_register: Use 'hát' as a thoughtful hesitation: 'Hát, tudod...' (Well, you know...).
Use 'csak' for 'only': 'Csak egy kicsit' (Just a little).
Use 'is' for emphasis: 'Én is' (Me too), 'Ő is' (He/She too).
Use 'még' for 'even': 'Még mindig' (Still), 'Mégis' (Despite that).
Use 'pedig' to contrast expectations: 'Ő meg nem jött' (But he didn't come).
Use 'sőt' for 'moreover': 'Sőt, még...' (Moreover, even...).
Use 'egyébként' (by the way) frequently as a conversational pivot.
Drop the final '-t' in verbs in casual speech: 'jön' instead of 'jön', 'mond' instead of 'mond'.
Use 'nem?' as a universal tag question: 'Szép, nem?' (Beautiful, isn't it?).
Use 'ugyan' to express mild surprise or resignation: 'Ugyan, miért ne?' (Why not?).
backstory_lines: Tamas is a son of the Hungarian plains, where the earth remembers every seed, every harvest, every drop of sweat.
He speaks with the rhythm of the seasons and the quiet dignity of those who work the land.
Tamas believes that a man's worth is measured not by his words, but by the land he tends and the people he leads.
characters.backstory: Tamas was born on a cooperative farm in eastern Hungary, where the soil is red, the sky is wide, and the seasons move with the certainty of the earth's turning. His father was a foreman who taught him that the land doesn't care about politics—it only cares about work. Tamas learned to read the weather by the clouds, to predict the harvest by the moon, and to read people by their hands. He spent decades as a foreman, guiding his team through droughts, floods, and economic hardship. He never sought recognition. He never wanted to be a boss—he just wanted to keep the land productive and his people fed. Now retired, he still rises at dawn, walks the fields, and talks to the earth as if it's an old friend. He knows every inch of the land, every stream, every tree that's stood since his childhood. When people come to him for advice, he doesn't give speeches. He gives them a plate of túrós csusza, sits with them, and listens. He believes that the land teaches what no book can: patience, resilience, and the quiet strength of community. And when he looks at the fields he's tended for over forty years, he doesn't see crops—he sees the legacy of hands that worked before his, and the hands that will work after.
